newsitem.title: USA: First witnesses expected in Oklahoma bombing case.
newsitem.headline: First witnesses expected in Oklahoma bombing case.

text.p: Prosecutors were set to begin introducing the first evidence and witnesses on Friday in the murder and conspiracy trial of accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh.

Jurors are expected to hear a tape recording of a city government meeting that convened across the street just minutes before the powerful truck bomb destroyed the Alfred P. Murrah building on April 19, 1995.

A massive roar can be heard, then screams and sirens, according to "The Daily Oklahoman" newspaper. Prosecutors and defence attorneys are forbidden to discuss the case due to a court-imposed gag order.

Also likely is testimony from a policeman who carried the body of one-year-old Baylee Almon from the building and handed her to a firefighter. A photograph of the lifeless child has since become world famous and won a Pulitzer prize.

And an employee of the Department of Housing and Urban Development who survived the blast is expected to list the 35 HUD employees who died -- the most fatalities in any federal agency in the building.
The prosecution and defence delivered opening salvos on Thursday in Denver federal court, giving a glimpse of what lies ahead in what should be a lengthy trial.
Chief prosecutor Joseph Hartzler said McVeigh, motivated by anti-government politics, blew up the federal building in hopes of provoking a right-wing "second American Revolution."

He revealed for the first time the existence of a file named ATFREAD that McVeigh allegedly created in his sister Jennifer's computer. The text rails at those who commit "treasonous actions" against the U.S. Constitution, saying "Die, you spineless cowardice bastards."

Prosecutors say McVeigh sought to avenge the 1993 FBI assault on the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, and was inspired by the extremist novel "The Turner Diaries" about a violent campaign to overthrow the U.S. government.
McVeigh carried a quote from the book when he was arrested just after the bombing, the prosecutor said.
"The real value of our attack today is in the psychological impact, not the immediate casualties," it said.

"He thought he would bring liberty to this nation," the prosecutor said in a narrative peppered with remarkable detail. On his way to pick up the rented truck for the bombing, for example, McVeigh was captured by a surveillance camera as he ate a hot apple pie in a fast-food restaurant, he said.
Defence attorney Stephen Jones tried to cast doubt on the government's case, asking, "Did they get the right man?"

He raised the specter of John Doe No. 2, a suspect who has never been identified nor captured. He cited the account of Dana Bradley, who recalls seeing a short, stocky, dark man get out of the rented truck just seconds before the blast. McVeigh is tall and fair-skinned.
Doctors had to crawl into the collapsed building and amputate Bradley's leg to free her from the rubble after the bombing. Bradley's mother and two young children died.
Of the government's handling of the evidence, the defence attorney said, "They contaminated it, mishandled it, abused it, manipulated it and engaged in forensic prostitution."
McVeigh, 29, has pleaded not guilty and could face the death penalty if convicted.
